utterances.text: Well, your answer earlier was: "Anyone in a uniform fighting for the Muslim army was an extremist." Isn't that your position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. Each and every person who attacked my village, no matter what the kind of uniform was that they were wearing - black, camouflage, green - for me those people were extremists. They were out to destroy my property, my village, and they succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's go back to Zekic and Arkan's Tigers briefly. Would you describe Arkan's Tigers as Serb extremists?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've heard about Arkan is that he was some sort of Mafia all over the world. What sort of an army he had and who was in that army or what they were doing, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Surely you're aware that Arkan's Tigers were a paramilitary group with a fearsome reputation for brutal ethnic cleansing of Muslims and not just a Mafia.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind everyone who was not a member of the TO or any other military formation must have been a member of a paramilitary unit or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you also aware that when Arkan's Tigers and Zekic entered Srebrenica they looted and burned and terrorised and killed Muslim civilians. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not something I'm aware of and I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you also aware that the Bratunac Crisis Staff used the killing of Zekic as a pretext to attack Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992, as a result of which 65 unarmed Muslim residents were murdered?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you even sure that it was Muslims who killed Goran Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what people were saying in the Serb villages at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could assist by placing a document on the ELMO. It's a lengthy document in the original, 20 pages or so, so we could only make a partial translation between now and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would be grateful, Mr. Stevanovic, if you could have a look at that document. Now, this is a criminal report which was sent, in fact, to the ICTY by Goran Zekic's father, which one can see from the face of the document. And we see the names of the people against whom the complaint is brought. You'll see the names Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik. Now, have you heard that Goran Zekic's father blamed the Serb leadership and Delivoje Sorak for killing his son? That he brought charges - including before this Tribunal - against Serbs for the killing of Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You maintain your opinion that Zekic was killed by Muslims, having seen that document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know better than his father who killed his son?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. I think the witness is clear about what he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if this could be made an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and received as Defence Exhibit D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 53. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you also said yesterday -- you referred yesterday as an incident provoking the conflict, that a Serb village, Oparci, was torched by Muslims. You also said you never entered the village but nonetheless you believe that it was torched by Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that it was torched by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that Muslim villages in your area were attacked by Serb forces at the same time, the same time period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Osmace yesterday as a purely Muslim village, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If D46 could be placed on the ELMO so we can see Osmace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D46, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you're looking at the exhibit, but Osmace isn't particularly far from your village, is it? If we can move it down a little bit more. You marked it yesterday, Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- I think the witness probably needs a minute since this is a new map to sort of orient himself with the particular village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Osmace is or was a Muslim village, wasn't it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him find it first, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you put your initials on top of the circle that you have just marked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you haven't answered the question. You haven't answered the question that was put to you. You've been asked whether Osmace is or was a Muslim village. So they are actually two questions in One. Is it a Muslim village now, and was it a Muslim village then, because I would imagine you're referring to the relative period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could now be shown Exhibit D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to two names on the list, they are at number 42 and at 157. If you look at that the first one refers to a Zoric, Nebojsa, from Sevojno [phoen] - I don't know if you see that - who was killed in Osmace on the 7th of May, 1992. Do you see that name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 42. Perhaps you can help us with this. Do you know where Sevojno is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sevojno. I know there's a place near Uzice that's called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We see that name. Now, if you look at number 157 we see a Milivoje Ilic in Brezani who was also killed in Osmace on the same day, the 7th of the May, 1992. Now, my question to you is this: You live in this area, Osmace isn't that far from you, do you have any idea why a soldier from Serbia and another soldier were getting killed in a Muslim village on the 7th of May, 1992, if they weren't attacking that village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they were killed in that village at all. It's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're saying that this document is in error, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that Osmace was attacked before Oparci was torched?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're saying it wasn't attacked, not that you don't know. You can state positively that it wasn't attacked, Osmace?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know back in my area that Oparci was attacked before any other villages were attacked. As for Osmace, it's far up there. I wasn't there; I didn't hear anything. I was not aware of it. Still it is my submission that Oparci was the first village to be burned and then the other Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you help us with whether the following Muslim villages were also attacked May and June? I'll read some names out: Jagodnja and Joseva on the 14th of May, 1992, the 22nd of May, 1992, and the 1st of June, 1992. Were you aware of attacks by Serb forces on Muslim villages on those dates?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to another place. Sikiric, if we can look at D46. If we can locate that on the map. You're familiar with Sikiric, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he have to mark it on the map or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you can move straight to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that in Sikiric 240 Muslims were expelled and it was attacked from the 31st of May to 2nd June, 1992, with 11 Muslims being killed. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally are you aware that Poloznic [phoen], Pirici, Zapolje, Podkorjen, Mocevici, Skenderovici, Diovici and Tegare were all attacked by Serb forces in May/June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally are you aware that Muslims were expelled from Fakovici in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fakovici, it's a Serb village, it's not a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're saying that there weren't any Muslims living in Fakovici before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have another document which we would be grateful if it can be placed on the ELMO. It's an extract from the 1991 census which we've seen before in this case. If you can look at that document, and you need to turn to the -- I think it's the third page. We see Fakovici near the top. And then the way this document works is you need to note the line, number 5, and then on the other page one sees the results of the 1991 census. Do you see there, Mr. Stevanovic, that according to that census there were 33 Muslims living in Fakovici in 1991, and 120 Serbs, so that nearly a quarter -- or more than a quarter of the population were Muslims. Does that change your answer or is this document also false?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is false, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I would be grateful if this document can be given an exhibit number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered and admitted as D54. One moment, Mr. Jones. I'm trying to follow you. But in the English version of this document under Fakovici in the 1981 sector under Croats you have nothing. Under Muslims you have nothing. Then under Serbs you have 149. Under Yugoslavs you have 4. And other -- others and unknown you have 5. I am not seeing any --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You need to turn the page to see the 1991 census, and the line is 5, line 5, total of 162; 33 Muslims, 122 Serbs, 6 Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. I see what you mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's the same in the original version. One has to turn over the page to see the 1991 results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, I see. Okay. I understand you better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So that we're clear. With respect to the answer the witness gave about the document being false, so that we're clear, it's the information as is contained as Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- pointed out is inaccurate, not that the document is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness's answer was very clear. I said is this document false? He said this document is false, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the population of Fakovici in 1991/1992, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Purely Serb. All were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The amount of people living there, the amount of inhabitants of Fakovici. And what do you understand by Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fakovici, I mean the village itself. As for the number of those who lived there, I'm not familiar with the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know how many houses there were in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I'm sorry. I can't be specific. I never counted the houses or the people. I went to school there, elementary school. That's all I did there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Mr. Jones, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stevanovic, yesterday when you were asked about incidents which led to a breakdown in relations between Serbs and Muslims you only mentioned incidents in which Serbs were victims. So my question is: Are you not aware of attacks, of killings and expulsions by Serbs of Muslims, or is it you chose not to mention them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Muslims in my area - in Sikirici, in Fakovici - in Fakovici there were no Muslims. In the Drina area, they wanted to go over to Mocevici and Osmace so that from there they could fire on all the Serb villages. They did this of their own free will and no one ever touched them, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that no crime was ever committed against a Muslim by a Serb, at least in your area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which period of time, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992 we can say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the destruction and burning of my village and the area which I lived, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're not just talking about your village. Yesterday you were talking about events in Oparci, in Zeleni Jadar, Srebrenica. So obviously you're aware of events in a broader area. So my question is: Are you aware that Serbs also committed crimes against Muslims, or is it your position that no such thing ever occurred in the first half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about the incidents at Jadar and Potocari the incidents involving Goran Zekic, and I know personally about this man who died in the backyard Milosav Milanovic; that was in late May. And those were the incidents that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me make it easier for you with one final question. Can you mention for us any incident where Muslims were victims or where they were attacked in the first half of 1992? Anything.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, there is a problem. We got the transcript stuck, so this usually takes a couple of minutes to adjust, so please bear with us, Mr. Jones. Mr. Stevanovic, I'm sorry for this interruption which is due to technical reasons, and I apologise to you, Mr. Jones, as well. I know that interruptions are not always welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had arrived, as far as the transcript is concerned, to a question which you were just putting to the witness. And you were asking the witness -- the witness had answered: Until the destruction and burning of my village and the area which I lived, nothing. And then it's you, Mr. Jones: We are not just talking about your village. Yesterday you were talking about events in Zeleni Jadar. You were aware -- you are aware of a broader area, are you aware that Serbs committed -- and I can recall what you asked and what he answered. Committed crimes against Muslims, and the witness from what I remember hearing told you: The only two instances I know is the killing of Goran Zekic and then he mentioned another name. I don't remember the name. Perhaps he can take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps I can put the question again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And maybe even more broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question is simply this, Mr. Stevanovic: Can you tell us of a single instant that you're aware of - and let's make it very broad - from the start of the war to the genocide in Srebrenica of the Muslims in July 1995, can you mention any incident --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- where you heard that Muslims were victims or attacked?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Let him answer the question because it's a very important question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you're asking me questions about a time when I wasn't there. There is no way I can answer these questions for you. I don't know what they're about. You're asking me about incidents having occurred about Muslims perpetrated by Serbs in April/May. In relation to that, I told you where I lived there were none as far as I was aware. I don't know about the broad area; therefore, there you have it. You're asking me about genocide and some other things when you have it clearly on the record that I was not even in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, it's -- the simple answer, Mr. Stevanovic, is that you're not aware of any crimes ever committed against Muslims by Serbs. I take that from your answer. You can answer yes or no. It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you some questions about the Bradjevina TO. Now, you told us yesterday that you were in the Bradjevina village guard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no TO in the village. There was only a group of people who stood guard and who protected their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, next door to you nearby is Grabovacka Rijeka, Vranesevici, right, and they have a village guard as well, do they not? They did in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vranesevici had none. Ruljevici had none. Only Bradjevina had one because we were the outermost villages, the outerlying villages. Down there on lower ground, people just kept working their land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't answer the question as regards Grabovacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did Grabovacka Rijeka have a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it did or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit D48.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that is a list or what at least purports to be a list for TO Grabovacka Rijeka, Vranesevici. Can you look at that document and the names and tell us whether that changes your answer as to whether there was a TO in Grabovacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no TO back then. They could have had village guards following the attack against Ratkovici and Oparci and after that man was killed in his own yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is this document also wrong in the information it contains that there was a TO in Grabovacka Rijeka? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The fact is, Mr. Stevanovic, isn't it, that the village guard is the same thing as the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you a series of documents. The first one dated 16th of April, 1992. I'll read the ERN number for the record. 00574584 to 00574585. If you look at that document. This concerns the establishment of the TO. It's dated the 16th of April, 1992. I'll draw your attention in particular to -- it's page 2 in the English, the decision. We see two paragraphs there. Firstly, the state of an imminent threat of war is hereby declared. And secondly, there's general public mobilisation of the TO in the entire territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And finally we see there that all military conscripts are duty-bound to make themselves available to the municipal TO staffs in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, if you look at that, my question for you is the following: This decision doesn't mention a village guard or village guards, and it's right, isn't it, that in fact after the 16th of April, 1992, all able-bodied men, Serbs, were conscripted into TOs?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, before the witness attempts to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe counsel is trying to elicit from the witness information about a village guard being mentioned in a document that I think will take the witness more than a minute or so to review. So if counsel is asking the witness to first review the document and see if there is no mention of the village guard, I think that that would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we can tell the witness -- since I am very familiar with this document myself, I can tell the witness that there is no mention of village guard anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he doesn't need to waste his time --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to looking for those words because he isn't going to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My point is precisely that there is no mention of a village guard in the document, that there were only TOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And actually the point that Mr. Jones is trying to make out of you, Mr. Stevanovic, is again whether you will agree that village guards are not mentioned here, or guards are not mentioned here because precisely they and the territory force -- territorial -- the TO were one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village guard and the Territorial Defence were never the same thing nor would they ever be. The village guard is only a group of people who sit around the village. These are small groups of people, nothing more than that. It's not the Territorial Defence. They don't belong to the Territorial Defence. These are people who are from their own village only. They were not mobilised, no such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You've got your answer, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I ask you this then: Why were those people exempted from a mobilisation which applied to all able-bodied Serbs in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had a timely mobilisation of the Territorial Defence taken place, I would have been the happiest man of all because I would have defended my house and I would have still had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if this document could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D55.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you also aware, Mr. Stevanovic, that when the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, was established, all TOs became part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Skelani I got a uniform with insignia of the Territorial Defence of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. So the TO was part of the Army of Republika Srpska? I'm not sure if your answer was heard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was your answer "da"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could place another exhibit on the ELMO. It's ERN 00408083 and it's a decision dated 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I draw your attention to Article 2 of that document where it said that: "Units and headquarters of the Territorial Defence are hereby renamed into commands and units of the army," that's the Bosnian Serb army, "the organisation and formations of which shall be determined by the president of the republic." And that's following the establishment of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is it right that that confirms what you've just told us, that the TO was part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if that document could also be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D56.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's also true, isn't it, Mr. Stevanovic, that all Serbs were mobilised into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: During what period of time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, that's a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In the first half of 1992. In fact, April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'll have to repeat your question. I've lost you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... have been mobilised into the VRS in 1992, because the VRS came into existence in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, there's a general mobilisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might assist if we put the next exhibit on the ELMO. I think it's D4 already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that this is an order of the republic of Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina - in fact the Bratunac Crisis Staff - dated the 16th of April, 1992, and it orders that all citizens who have come of age were to be mobilised without any upper age limit and it's in fact not even confined to men. And further on one sees that persons who didn't answer the call were -- faced arrest. Now, were you aware of that mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're putting questions to me here as if I wrote these orders, as if I sent them to villages, to people, and mobilised them. I keep telling you the same thing. There was no mobilisation in my area in that time, in that period, from the beginning of 1992 until my village was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your answer is that in fact although -- your answer is that there was no mobilisation in your area before June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there wasn't any mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would Your Honours bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could place another document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have -- or is it been tendered -- it's been tendered already?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. It's D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now the next document is 01785256 and it's dated 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stevanovic, are you aware of where Milici is first of all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, according to this document the public security station were to arrest draftees who didn't respond to the invitation to join the Serb army. My question is: Are you not aware that at that time Serbs who were -- did not answer the call were being arrested by the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were only captured by the Yugoslav police on the other side of the Drina and the military police, and they were the ones who returned them. As for the Serbs themselves in Republika Srpska, there were all sorts of things going on, people were trying to escape. Nobody could force them to fight, nobody could catch them, and nobody had the right to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So people were trying to escape the draft?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who did escape did escape, and those who didn't, didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you accept that there was a draft?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue any orders for mobilisation or anything, and I do not know anything about this. I don't know anything about Milici. And after the war, after all these problems, I go up there above Sarajevo to Pale, to Milici to work there as a construction worker. I don't know who this commander is. I don't know anything about this. I lived in the village of Ratkovici, or rather the village of Bradjevina, not in Milici or anywhere else that far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if that document could be given an exhibit number as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D57. Is that correct, registrar? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, moving to your village at the time of the attack on the 27th of June, 1992, you had an automatic gun, machine-gun, didn't you, on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not have a machine-gun. I had a Smajser, an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And it's right, isn't it, that the other men in the Bradjevina village guard also had weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Stanisa Stevanovic had one rifle, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll be grateful if the witness can be shown a copy of his 2001 statement which he made to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First of all, I will ask: Do you recall making a statement to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Skelani. I gave a statement to someone who came. I don't know who this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that statement, and I'll direct your attention in the Serbian version to the second page -- it's actually the first page but it says 2. The bottom paragraph. And there it's right, isn't it, that you say: "We had commenced a village guard which would patrol our homes during the night but we were not armed as none of us were hunters, so we didn't have any weapons." Do you recall making that statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but before the witness answers this question I would just like to state with respect to this issue, I provided proofing notes with corrections to the ICTY statement with respect to this issue to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, corrections. We, of course, don't accept that these are corrections or anything of that nature. I'm quite properly putting to this witness the fact that he said something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not aware of these corrections in any case. Go ahead with the question. I'm pretty sure that if he could explain to you he can explain to us. In any case he has already given evidence as to who went to procure these weapons and from where.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you made that statement and you made it stating that it was a truthful statement and that you signed it. Now, do you remember saying that, that the village guard did not have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am answering the questions that you put to me here, and I answer the same question several times and you still don't understand what I'm saying and you're asking the same questions again. How can I know? I mean, why would I say that I had a weapon and then I say that I did not have a weapon? What reason is there for me to say that kind of thing? I said quite clearly what the situation was with weapons, so what kind of a question is this now? I don't really understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question to you is: Why did you say to an investigator of this Tribunal that the village guard did not have any weapons when in fact you did have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood the question. Maybe I thought that this person asked me about the entire village guard. I myself did have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I did think it was a matter worth pursuing a little further. This is a statement taken by a professional investigator of the Tribunal, and it is very clear that this is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So my next question is: Why did you lie in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't allow you. He himself has just explained to you that he may have not understood the question that was being asked of him. That he probably understood that the question related to the entire guard. Why do you attribute lying to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because it's a very clear statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- come on, no. Move to the next question but I will not allow you to put this question to him or the way you put it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, please, where you got your weapons from since you weren't hunters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered this question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you like, Your Honour, I can lead him on -- a bit further on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Jovanovic, the owner of the Medina restaurant cafe in Fakovici, and are you aware that he was distributing weapons to Serbs in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Jovanovic? I knew him, but I do not know that he distributed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware then that many Serbs in the Fakovici area got their weapons from Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it is right, isn't it, that in 1992 - let's say in June 1992 - many more Serbs were armed than they were in, say, 1991 or 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question. I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'll rephrase it. Isn't it right that Serbs in your area were in fact arming themselves in the first half of 1992 in preparation for conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, whoever had money tried to get a weapon and bought a weapon. Where they bought weapons and from who is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that you were a member of the SDS. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you know Slavko Jovanovic also through the SDS, I presume?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS, no. I don't know him through the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also told us that you didn't pay any dues to this -- to the SDS. Is that right? And if so, why were you exempted from paying dues?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I never paid any dues because nobody ever asked me to pay any. I was only a member of the SDS. As for payment, no one ever asked me for any such thing nor ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that capacity as a member of the SDS in that area, you're aware, are you not, that the SDS organised a training camp in Ruljevici?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if you could be shown P407, the map, and if you could mark Ruljevici on the map. I could probably help the witness. It's a bit further down. Perhaps if you look to the right of Vranesevici and down a little bit. Well, if you can't find it on the map, then not to worry. It's near you, isn't it, Ruljevici, it's near Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it possible that there could have been a training camp there for soldiers and that you would be unaware of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just have a time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Which period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in the first half of 1992 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992. And the question is: "Is it possible that there could have been a training camp there for soldiers and that you would be unaware of it"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. But this belongs to the Bratunac municipality, not the Srebrenica municipality, you see. Or perhaps there was something going on that they tried to hide away from the people, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you meant a Serb -- a Serbian training camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When Mr. Jones put the question to you, he was referring to a Serbian training camp and your answer remains as it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The answer is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Staying with P407 and looking again at Mocevici, if you could locate that on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. We all know where it is and he has located it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mocevici is up in the hills, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's also right, isn't it, that some of the villages you pointed out and which you've circled on the map - Oparci, Magudovici, Dvoriste, Ducici - were all Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's also right, isn't it, that in June 1992, if you're a Muslim from Mocevici, because of these tensions you couldn't simply walk into the Ratkovici or Dvoriste or you would risk getting shot by the village guard on a patrol? In any event, you couldn't pass freely as a Muslim from Mocevici into Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure this question is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness was about to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let him answer and let's see whether he has understood the question or not, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean a Muslim coming to any one of these Serb villages, of course any person could come to any one of these villages, sit there, talk to people, go and do whatever. I mean, if that was the intention of the person who was coming. Or the other way around. A Serb could go to visit them, or a Muslim could come and visit us. Do you understand? Until the killings started. Once the killings started, no one went to see anyone any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking to. You've referred to incidents in May and perhaps in early June. If we talk about the period just before the attack on your village, when there had been killings, when there were tensions, it's right, isn't it, that a Muslim in Mocevici could not just freely pass into these Serb villages without risking his life?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would be grateful if my learned friend would cease interrupting. In fact, I'm waiting for the interpretation; that's he delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. Go ahead with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Dvoriste where the man was killed, I don't think that it would have crossed any Muslim's mind to go to that village at that time. As for Bradjevina, Magudovici, they could always come, and they came as they came, with weapons, and they started killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The fact is, isn't it, as we can see on this map, that Mocevici was surrounded by Serb villages, certainly in June 1992, and it's right also, isn't it, that Muslim refugees from the places I mentioned earlier - Tegare, Pirici, and Zapolje - were in that area and were unable to move freely?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mocevici was never surrounded by Serb villages. All these Serb villages are in a valley below Mocevici towards Drina. And there were never any Muslim villages. There are mixed villages. Mocevici are further up in relation to us. And then all the way to Srebrenica there are Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So Muslims in Mocevici would not be able to pass to the Drina, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they wouldn't be able to go to Fakovici, they wouldn't be able to go to get provisions from the stores in Fakovici? They were stuck where they were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Mocevici had a road leading to Srebrenica, Bjelovac, Sase, and all these other places. There was never a road for a motor vehicle or any kind of bigger vehicle between Bradjevina, Ratkovici, Mocevici. There are only these three or four Serb villages that had no road, and we only had a road to Grabovacka Rijeka. Nowhere else. We were the only ones that were cut off. At any moment they could go through these villages. People went to the market. They took their cattle to Fakovici and back. I don't know what you mean when you say they couldn't pass there when they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically the witness is also telling you, Mr. Jones, that if they couldn't go to Fakovici, they could go in the opposite direction and get supplies from other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In relation to that, isn't it the case, Mr. Stevanovic, that at this time, June 1992, Muslims could not go to Srebrenica because the Serbs held Pribicevac, Sase, and Brezani on the other side and therefore prevented them from passing through to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the Serb villages were at risk and were surrounded and Muslims had a road open to go to Srebrenica or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask you about Magudovici. That's a neighbouring hamlet of Bradjevina, isn't it, and it's something like 300 to 500 metres away from Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right that before the 27th of June, 1992, there was an armed infantry unit and observation post at Magudovici and artillery, namely a 120-millimetre gun?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're saying that there was no infantry unit, no observation post, and no artillery in Magudovici in this period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our observation posts, to put it that way, those were a trench here and there in the village. You could observe from there because Mocevici -- from Mocevici you could see the village across the way. I'm not sure what you mean when you say "observation post." I saw no observation posts in the area, or weapons for that matter, nor did I notice any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just about to move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can take the break. Now, how much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Approximately another hour I would say, perhaps a bit less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will have to cut that down because we only have three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Plus we have some questions, too. So let's have a 25-minute break. All right. And you have a re-examination as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do in fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will need to regulate that. Allow us five minutes for ourselves. How much do you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this moment I require 10 minutes based on what counsel has elicited so far. And if he continues to go into other areas, I might find it necessary to re-examine. But at the moment it's 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This witness is going definitely to finish today. There is no way we will allow him to come again next time. So that leaves us 15 minutes at the maximum for Prosecution and ourselves. Basically, that leaves you with half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So try to -- 25 minutes, and please try to be punctual, all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now about the finding of Stojan Stevanovic on the 27th of June, 1992. I'm going to refer you again to your -- the statement you made in 2001, and you'll be shown a copy of that statement. And in the English version it's page 3, bottom three paragraphs. In the Bosnian version it's also page 3, bottom three paragraphs, carrying on to the next page. Now, if you would read just to yourself where it starts in English: "We then decided to escape using the bushes for cover as we went along the brook towards the stream which leads down to the Drina river." If you read there down -- and there's the next couple of paragraphs. What I'll do is rather than reading all of that I'll summarise the main points and ask you some questions about what you said in 2001 about finding Stojan Stevanovic. Now, according to that statement: On the 27th of June, 1992, after the attack on Bradjevina, you and other men went to Grabovacka Rijeka and then you came back several hours later, around 6.00 or 7.00 p.m. And when you left Bradjevina, you didn't know that Stojan was dead, but when you came back to Bradjevina you discovered that he had been killed. And in fact you found him at the corner, I think it was, of Zivko Stevanovic's house. You found him. And also according to what you said then in 2001, Stanisa Stevanovic left 15 minutes before you to go back to Bradjevina from Grabovacka Rijeka. Before he left he didn't say anything about Stojan being dead. And in fact, he had been in Fakovici that day getting food. Do you see that in your statement? The last part: "At this time I was with Stanisa Stevanovic who had been in Fakovici that day getting food from the only store." So Stanisa had not in fact even been in Bradjevina during the attack. So my question to you is: Isn't it right that in fact you didn't know that Stojan Stevanovic was dead until you returned to Bradjevina in the evening. And Stanisa was in Fakovici all day on the day of the attack. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I was next to my house, I didn't see where Stanisa was at the time nor where Stojan was once I was back from Grabovacka Rijeka. Back there they had told me that people had left for Bradjevina to pull people out, those who had survived. And then I returned towards Bradjevina. I met Stanisa at the way into the village of Vranesevici. He was pushing a cart ahead of him, and he told me that Stojan had been found with his throat cut in the middle of the village next to Zivko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First of all, Stanisa had been in Fakovici that day getting food. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The village of Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then why did you say to the investigator: "This time I was with Stanisa Stevanovic who had been in Fakovici that day getting food"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said at the time I saw Stojan, Stanisa was pushing a cart, and with him I came to Grabovacka Rijeka. And with those people who were with Stanisa, Borivoje Milanovic and Sreten Stjepanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question was: Why did you say Stanisa was in Fakovici that day getting food from the only store if that wasn't the case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So are you saying that the investigator wrongly recorded that fact?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You signed this statement, didn't you, and it was read to you in your language?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the statements were read back. I might as well have signed a hundred different statements as well as this one. I probably didn't read all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You described Stanisa today as just a person, but in fact he's more than that, isn't he? He's a relative of yours and he's lived in the same hamlet as you for all your life. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said a person. Am I supposed to say that in relation to each person, if we're related or not. Of course he's a person. What else should he be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You can tell us now whether he is a relative of yours and if so what sort of a relative.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stanisa is a relative. There were 12 families in my family, six of them called Milanovic and six called Stevanovic. There were only two families in that village, and of course all these Stevanovics were related in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't what's happened is that Stanisa has spoken to you and told you that he's changed his story about finding Stojan and he's now asked you to change your story, too?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you referred also in your 2001 statement and also today to people who died on the 27th of June, 1992. And that's on page 5 of your statement, at least in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if the witness can be shown D45. If that could be placed on the ELMO -- yes, on the ELMO is best.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this document, this is a list of killed soldiers from the military post Bratunac. And I'm going to ask you to look at line 557 first of all. And I think you'll see there Stojan Stevanovic, number 557, son of Dragomir. That's the Stojan you've referred to today, isn't it, killed on the 27th of June, 1992, in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the village of Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if I could refer you to number 125 on the list. You'll see the name there Ljubisa Gajic born in Ratkovici and who died in Ratkovici on the 27th of June, 1992. And is that the same Ljubisa Gajic, son of Predrag, that you've referred to today? Born in 1966 in Ratkovici. So it should be line 125. Is that the Ljubisa Gajic who you referred to today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now number 550. You can see Novica Stanojevic. Is it right that he's the son of Vitomir born in Magudovici and died on the 27th of June, 1992, according to that, in Magudovici?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all killed in Magudovici or in Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to look at number 435 on the list. We see there the name Vladimir Pavlovic, also died on the 27th of June, 1992, in Magudovici Brdo. Now, you referred to someone called Vukoman, the nickname Vlado, but is that the person you're referring to, Vladimir, son of Obrad? Is that the Vlado Pavlovic you referred to as dying on the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlastimir Pavlovic, not Vukoman or Vlado.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But my question to you: Is that the same person that you referred to today as Vlado? Vladimir Pavlovic, son of Obrad, as one of the people who died on 27th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Vlastimir and his nickname was Vlado.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally I'll refer you to line 234. There we have Rado Jovanovic who died in Bradjevina on the 27th of June, 1992. Now, would that be the Rade Jovanovic who you referred to in your 2001 statement from Stanatovici?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rade Jovanovic, but I don't know his father's name. The one who was killed in Bradjevina, his name was Rade Jovanovic, that's how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's right, isn't it, that out of the six or so people you mentioned who died on the 27th of June, 1992, that at least four of them were soldiers of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them were, those who were killed, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So again, is the information contained in this document false according to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's false.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you think why the VRS would invent a document, invent information, which is false? Can you think of any explanation for why that would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. This calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just going back to Gajic briefly, Ljubisa Gajic, if you look again at your 2001 statement. And in English it's page 4, paragraph 5. There you say that you were told that Ljubisa Gajic had been seen: "Been killed on the road and shot with a sniper rifle, that he died and then his body was set alight." Whereas today you've told us that he was burned alive. And my question to you is: You've changed your account today, have you not, to exaggerate the circumstances under which Mr. Gajic died?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So which is the correct account? The one in your 2001 statement or what you've said today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Gajic was not killed on any road. It's an unsealed road, a dirt track. That's all it is He was burned alive tied to a cornstalk. I heard him scream. I heard him cry for help. Milutin, who watched all the while, told me that this man Ramco was there and had seen him. And he said: But Ljubisa is walking down the road like King Marko. That's what he said. He said: I'll have his mother now. And then he fired at him and he wounded him. And that was the voice I heard. And what Milutin said was the truth. They tied him to a cornstalk after that. Whether he was alive or dead, at that time I don't know. Whether he was alive or dead by the time he was burned alive tied to a cornstalk.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, you don't know any of this firsthand, do you? It's all what you've been told?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you now about the conversation which you say you had with a Nezir Jakubovic in Skelani. You described him as a young man. How old would you say he is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So he would have been about 18 during the war -- during the attack on your village in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So he's certainly not someone who is more in the region of 59 years old? You're not mistaken about his age to that extent?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I possibly be mistaken about something like that? I don't know what his age was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you another document. If that could be placed on the ELMO. And it's an extract from the census. Now, if you look at this document, it's page 3, line -- the third line from the bottom. You see a Nezir Jakubovic who according to this was born in 1945. So that's not the person you're talking about, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person on the list that I talked about, I don't think that's the same person. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll refer you now to the first page of this document where there's a -- in the third line a Mucin Jakubovic from Mocevici and ask you to look further down the page and you see what I think may be his children; in any event, a Zikrit Jakubovic [phoen], a Majro Jakubovic [phoen], and Mirzad Jakubovic [phoen] from Mocevici. It's not any of those people who you claim to have spoken to, is it, in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were not the people that I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but could we -- there's no title to this document. Does counsel have any information? We've been given a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He said it is from the census. What is this document exactly, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's from the 1991 census and it's listing persons with that name, Jakubovic. Yes, all the Jakubovics in the village Mocevici and Skenderovici. So I was drawing the witness's attention to the one, Nezir Jakubovic, that appears on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say that Nezir told you that Akif commanded the attack on your village on the 27th of June and that he was an associate of Zulfo of Naser Oric. Now, that you said he told you by him, according to you. If that information was wrong, you wouldn't know, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know who were Mr. Oric's associates or assistants. I only know what Nezir told me, that Akif commanded the operation against Bradjevina and that these two persons were close associates of Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be D58.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally you've told us that you were in Serbia for much of the war and that you were not in the VRS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you maintain that you weren't in the 3rd Battalion, 4th Infantry Company of the Bratunac Brigade in 1993, 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown another couple of documents. One I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this first document you're being shown a list of persons in the reserve force of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, 4th Infantry Company. If you look at number 15 you see Milenko Stevanovic, son of Radivoje. Your father is Radivoje, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Radivoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it says that you were a platoon commander in the 3rd Infantry Battalion, 4th Infantry Company. Is there something funny, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's funny. I never held any kind of rank nor was I ever a member of that unit. So, yes, the whole thing seems strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can that document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be D59.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this last document I'm afraid we only have one copy because we retained it at the last minute. If it's put on the ELMO, then at least everyone can see it. We'll do our utmost to provide a translation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's this document, to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think my colleague might be able to explain a bit better. I'll hand over to her for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a list of payments in relation to the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995. Can the usher please turn to page 1 of the document and it will explain itself. And then perhaps the interpreters can read from the ELMO. It's a list, military post 7042, in relation to the month of July 1995. Therefore, this is a list in relation to military post 7042 for the month of July 1995. And this number is in relation to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I would hate to interrupt, but if we don't have a copy of this document or unless I'm mistaken, could we at least be shown, the Prosecution, the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're seeing it there. He's only got one copy and copies will be made and distributed later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the page, to the relevant page, where there appears to be the name of Stevanovic, Radivoje and Milenko, and then KV, which is commander of the platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So my question again to you, Mr. Stevanovic, is: Do you maintain still that you were not a member of the Bratunac Brigade at any time during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I abide by that and it is simply true that I was never a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you maintain that you weren't in Potocari in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is my submission that I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. I'll just confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What are we going to do with this document? Are you going to tender that particular document in evidence or do you want to photocopy it and then tender the photocopy because it's marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the latter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The latter. So we take it that document will be -- yes, will be received in evidence to be marked as Defence Exhibit D60, D60. We will all have copies of the document. Mr. Siller will be taking care of that so we don't even have to worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson, go head. You have 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you, Mr. Jones. I forgot to thank you for even finishing earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, counsel just suggested to you that you and Stanisa had gotten together to get your stories, I believe is how he put it, straight or say the same or similar thing. Could you tell us when was the last time you saw Stanisa. Did you see him prior to coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you live in Skelani. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where does he live?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grabovacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was the last time you had seen him prior to coming to The Hague, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him sometime in July because I went to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you saw him, did you have a copy of the ICTY statement with you when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whose statement? His or the other ones?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have a copy of your ICTY statement that you gave to the investigator in 2001 with you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never had that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when is the first time you saw your ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you met with me. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you were asked to read the statement and indicate whether it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, point out to me a number of inaccuracies in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Without going through all of them, but you did indicate that contrary to the ICTY statement the village guard did have two guns?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also talked about finding -- excuse me. You also made reference to the body of Stojan Stevanovic and that you indicated that you did not find the body, which is what is stated in your statement, but in fact you came across Stanisa who already had the body. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in fact, another inaccuracy was the fact that your statement stated that you didn't personally see the whole village burned to the ground, but -- as was indicated in your statement, but this was what was told you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to information when counsel inquired earlier about what information you had about crimes being committed against Muslims. Do you recall that line of questioning? Well, I'm rephrase the question. In 1992 how did you receive information about what crimes were being committed in your area? And this is with respect to either crimes against Serbs or crimes against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the press and Radio Yugoslav. They published that over the radio at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And they only published crimes against Serbs, not crimes against Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you went to Serbia in January of 1993, you indicated that you stayed until Dayton in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you were in Serbia, did the Serb media, either television or newspaper, report crimes committed against Muslims or did they also commit crimes -- I'm sorry. Did they only report crimes against Serbs or did they report crimes committed against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Sometimes when things happened elsewhere they carried that, too. It depends on what a given TV station could get hold of, what reports. Sometimes they reported on what was going on around Sarajevo, the Krajina, or in the Banja Luka area, that sort of thing. I was not familiar with any of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And did that newspaper media report any crimes committed against Muslims say, for instance, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't about crimes; it was about fierce fighting going on. That's what they talked about. But not really about individual crimes, no reports that I came across at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did they report crimes against Serbs -- committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything was done the same way. Serbs, Muslims, or what happened and where. That's what the TV reported on. I didn't really watch TV much in those days. It was only what I caught every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who did you rely on for information other than watching TV every so often? Did you rely on anyone else for information?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relatives would sometimes tell me things. Someone would come over and they would tell us about what was happening in a different village. For example, in the Fakovici area I heard that Fakovici had come under attack and had been torched. I didn't exactly see this for myself. This was information that came from people who were refugees from that area, and whoever crossed over into Serbia would tell those stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: As you sit here today, Mr. Stevanovic, have you heard of crimes being committed against Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Whether -- I'm not asking you whether it's true. Have you heard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard in the media that people were getting killed and were dying all over the place. Now, I had no information about specific crimes other than people getting killed in fighting perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to what counsel suggested to you earlier, that the village guard and the Territorial Defence is the same organisation, you have been a member of the village guard in Bradjevina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you were a member of the Territorial Defence in Skelani. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what is the difference -- and maybe I could lead just a little bit because we are --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If Your Honour would allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need the explanation. He's already explained it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
