utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My final question to you: Is there a difference without telling us in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He already said so. If you go back to the transcript he explained what the village guards were and it had absolutely nothing to do with the territorial force or TO as they are known. I don't think we need really any further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the mobilisation, and you were shown document -- I'm not going to show it to you at the moment, but there was a legal decision that counsel showed you that talked about mobilisation of Serb military men. Did anyone come to your village and give you this decision or told you in June 1992 or prior that you had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had there been an actual decision, I would have had to receive this call-up paper. And this would have been somebody's official duty to come and inform me. Nobody informed me and I did not receive any such call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did anyone come to your village to arrest you or any other of the men of military age during that period of time for not serving in the military?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one came.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And finally, just with respect to your discussion with the individual in Skelani on the 26th of October, is it correct that this individual confirmed certain information with respect -- certain information about the attack in Bradjevina that you yourself had prior knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, "confirmed," I don't know where counsel is getting that from. That hasn't been given in evidence. He said in fact in cross-examination that the only information he had was from this individual. So I'm not really sure what the purpose of the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. Rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This individual gave you information about the attack in Bradjevina that he had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we haven't heard your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He personally talked to me in the coffee bar and we sat together and had a drink.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he discussed with you -- he mentioned that he saw the body of Stojan, your cousin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what he told you about the body, was it similar to your observations of Stojan's body when you saw it in Bradjevina in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Stojan on the actual spot. I saw him on the outskirts of the village when Stanisa was transporting him in the wheelbarrow. I saw that his throat had been slit. And he told me that he had seen Stojan in the middle of the village with his throat slit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So this information that you received from him was similar to what you yourself observed - that's my question - about Stojan's injuries? Secondly, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to Ljubisa, did the information he gave you about Ljubisa and how he died, is that similar to what you previously knew about Ljubisa and how he died?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please conclude, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. At this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt from Denmark would like to put some questions to you. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. This case is about the attack on your village in June 1992. And you explained that there was soldiers, Muslim soldiers, and Muslim civilians who attacked you but that for you it was one in the same thing. Could you describe to me how was what you called the soldiers like? About their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had camouflage green uniforms, black uniforms, forest keepers uniforms, the clothing that forest keepers used to wear in forests before. There were civilians, wearing civilian clothes. Everyone who carried a weapon and went out there to destroy everything I had is all the same to me. They are all attackers, regardless of whether they were women, regardless of whether they were old men, young men. They were killing people, slaughtering, destroying. What other word can I use for them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: If you should try to describe to me those who you would call soldiers, were they under order, were they disciplined? Did they just go together with what you call the civilians in one group or various groups but without any distinction?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the approaches to the village and during the attack against the village, I noticed more people wearing uniforms. Behind them was the second wave of people wearing uniforms and wearing civilian clothes. So there were two formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And the first formation, was that under order, so to speak? Could you see that they went according to an order in a specific way, or was it just as when the second group came, the second wave as you say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were walking towards my house along the meadows and creeks. They would shoot, they would get closer, they would lie down, they would get up -- get even closer. And that's how they ultimately reached the house and the yard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Last question. In January -- early January 1993 when you in Skelani actually became a member of the Territorial Defence and you got a rifle and you got a uniform, what happened to that rifle and uniform later in January when you left Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Muslims attacked Skelani there was total disarray among the Serbs. Everybody threw away their weapons, whatever, and everybody tried to get out. There was weapons along the road. You could pick up as many as you liked. People would just throw them away. They did not believe that they could defend themselves. And the Muslims did not manage to enter Skelani because of the neighbouring villages. And then the Serbs regrouped and then they relaunched an offensive. At that moment, or rather the next day after the attack -- I can't remember exactly whether it was the second day or whether it was the very next day, then I went over to Bajina Basta. I never went back. I was not pleased with the command or with the people who were in command there. We were all left to our own devices without any command or proper discipline. I left and I never went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could you remember what happened -- I understand that you threw your rifle away, but what happened to your uniform? Did you keep that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one could enter the territory of Yugoslavia wearing a uniform. I had a red sweater on, civilian clothing. My trousers were black, some kind of dark trousers. So I had to wear civilian clothes when going from the territory of Yugoslavia to Republika Srpska and also from Republika Srpska to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser from Germany would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have two questions. Mr. Stevanovic, there have been quite a few questions where you answered I do not know, I am not aware. Now, when you have been asked with regard to the ethnic set-up of Fakovici, you would say: There are no Muslims, there have been no Muslims. How could you be so sure that there were no Muslims? How did you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Fakovici. I went there to elementary school for four years. I was at that school for four years, and I know that there is only Serbs in Fakovici. As for Zanjevo, as it's called nowadays, it's used to be called Abdulici before, that's what the map says, that was a neighbouring village to Fakovici. That was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Another question refers to the talk which you had in Skelani just a month ago with regard to the attack. You said you have been told that Akif took over command from Naser, he said, and he was in charge of this particular attack. What does it mean, took over command? Does it mean that Naser was substituted by Akif or that Akif had received a command from Naser? How was it meant or how do you mean it was meant?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me fully. Naser issued an order to Akif and Akif led that unit, these Muslims that attacked these Serb villages. It's not that he took over his command. He was loyal to Naser Oric. He carried out his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I asked you because the English translation may not have been completely clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I have a final question. And again it relates to this meeting you had very recently with Nezir, the person who introduced himself to you as Nezir Jakubovic. More or less I would like an explanation from you as to how he could know who was Stojan Stevanovic, who was Slavko Petrovic, and who was Novica Stanojevic. How could he -- I can understand maybe with regard to Stojan Stevanovic, but with regard to the other two? How could you sit down with someone, discuss the events of 1992, and literally this man would tell you: Yes, I remember Stojan Stevanovic with his throat slit. I remember Novica. Can you explain to me how the conversation went?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation, from the very beginning, I put questions to him and then he gave me answers. As for how come they knew people's names and who was who, Mocevici and Bradjevina from the Second World War cooperated -- were engaged in agriculture together, went to work for each other, paid each other per diems. There was a store called Zeljo Hajrudin's store in Mocevici, and that was our favorite store. We Serbs from the neighbouring villages went to that store in Mocevici. So we all know each other. We're neighbours. He also worked at Novica's father's farm. As for Magudovici and Mocevici, also their fields border each other, their pastures, their meadows. There was cooperation. Everybody knew each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, as I understand you, it's not that you have drawn a conclusion to who he was referring to, but that during the discussion that you had with him he specifically mentioned to you the names Stojan Stevanovic or Slavko Petrovic or Novica. He mentioned the names himself, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That brings us to the end of your testimony. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, on behalf of the Tribunal, and on my own behalf, I should like to thank you for coming over to give testimony in this trial. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher and you will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of everyone here, we wish you all a safe journey back home. Thank you. That brings us to an end. We will resume on the 22nd. In the meantime, you will all be doing all the homework that we have been discussing about earlier. Thank you.
